parts.title: [PART 1] My uncle's lawyer asked why I brought wet wipes to the reading of his will
parts.story_so_far: At Uncle Leo's will reading, Cousin Trevor presents a brand-new notarized addendum claiming 90% of the estate. As the lawyer slides it across the table, the narrator pulls out a cheap wet wipe to test the ink.

lines.text: My uncle's lawyer asked why I brought a pack of wet wipes to the reading of his will.
Uncle Leo spent forty years repairing vintage wristwatches, and he had two habits everyone in our family knew by heart.
He signed every single legal document left-handed with the same teal fountain pen, and he never trusted my cousin Trevor with a house key.
Three days before Uncle Leo passed in hospice, Trevor suddenly showed up at the hospital with a mobile notary he found on a classifieds board.
I didn't say a word in the hallway, I just kept the unopened birthday card Uncle Leo had mailed me two weeks earlier inside my coat pocket.
When we walked into the law office on Thursday morning, Trevor was already wearing Leo's vintage gold watch on his wrist.
He tossed a printed brochure for a vacation rental management company onto the mahogany table and grinned at me across the chairs.
He told me not to worry about mowing the lake house anymore because he was turning the place into a short-term rental by next Friday.
The estate lawyer cleared his throat, adjusted his glasses, and slid a single freshly notarized addendum across the desk.
According to that one page, Uncle Leo had left ninety percent of everything he owned directly to Trevor.
Trevor leaned back with his arms crossed and told the lawyer to hurry up and stamp the transfer paperwork.
I asked the lawyer if I could verify my uncle's signature line up close before anyone filed it with probate.
The lawyer nodded, so I reached into my coat pocket, tore open the cheap packet of wet wipes, and pressed one damp corner directly onto the final letter of Uncle Leo's name. [pause]
When I lifted my thumb, the lawyer stared at the paper and his face went completely sheet-white.

card.title: PART 1 | My uncle's lawyer asked why I brought wet wipes to the reading of his will.

card.body: Showing up to a will reading already wearing the deceased man's watch tells you everything you need to know.

parts.title: [PART 2] Fresh fountain ink bleeds under moisture—laser-printed forged signatures don't move a millimeter
parts.story_so_far: The narrator presses a wet wipe onto the signature line of Trevor's notarized addendum, leaving the lawyer pale.

lines.text: Fresh fountain ink bleeds under moisture, while laser-printed forged signatures don't move a millimeter.
Trevor jumped halfway out of his chair and yelled that I had just ruined an official legal document.
I didn't blink—I pulled Uncle Leo's birthday card out of my coat pocket and touched the same wet wipe to his signature inside the card.
Within two seconds, the real teal ink feathered into a soft blue smudge across the white paper.
Then I turned the notarized addendum toward the overhead lamp so the lawyer could see the glossy toner sitting flat on top of the cotton sheet.
Trevor had scanned Uncle Leo's real signature off an old check, resized it in a free editor, and printed it onto fancy resume paper before paying a shady notary to stamp the bottom.
When Trevor tried to snatch the paper off the desk, the lawyer slammed his palm flat over the signature line and called his senior partner on speaker.

Better yet, I played the voicemail from Uncle Leo's credit union manager from two weeks earlier, confirming Leo had personally frozen every change to his estate file unless two witnesses and his attorney were present in person. [laugh]
The senior partner walked in three minutes later with building security right behind him.
The lawyer quietly told Trevor that attempting to probate a forged testamentary instrument in our state is a felony, and he had thirty seconds to decide what stayed on the table.
Trevor didn't say another word—he unclasped Uncle Leo's vintage gold watch, set it beside the damp wet wipe, and walked out beside two security guards.
Probate wrapped up two months later under Leo's original will, and I still keep that cheap packet of wet wipes right next to his fountain pen on my desk.

card.title: PART 2 | Fresh fountain ink bleeds under moisture—laser-printed forged signatures don't move a millimeter.

card.body: Water-based fountain ink vs. fused laser toner is an instant tell under any desk lamp.

reply.body: And grabbing at the document in front of two attorneys is basically a confession.
